newsitem.title: Netherlands: EU WATERS DOWN TREATY AS TALKS PLOUGH ON.
newsitem.headline: EU WATERS DOWN TREATY AS TALKS PLOUGH ON.

text.p: European Union leaders watered down an already modest proposal for a new EU treaty on Tuesday as a raft of national concerns blocked what had been left of ambitions for the next step in European integration.
Diplomats said the negotiations were running behind schedule and some delegations warned that the talks, on the second day of the EU's mid-year summit, could run well into late evening.

The leaders discussed the treaty -- designed to prepare the bloc for enlargement into eastern Europe and to make it more meaningful to its citizens -- over lunch, but most progress had been in diluting earlier proposals.
Britain, Ireland and Denmark were given opt-outs from parts of the treaty in a move that leaders hoped would propmt closer cooperation in crime fighting and immigration policy.

France gave up on its long-held desire for the appointment of a high-level figure to steer EU foreign policy, agreeing with the rest that a senior, but relatively obscure, Eurocrat should take on the task instead.

National sensitivities, meanwhile, ensured that the veto would remain in areas of asylum, immigration and refugee policy, a blow to those who have argued over the 15 months of talks that majority voting is necessary for the bloc to be effective.

Under the latest draft treaty, EU countries would agree to cooperate more closely in areas such as asylum, immigration, visa policy and crime fighting. Breaking from current practice, the European Commission would be allowed to recommend rules.
The Schengen accord, linking most of the bloc's members in a partially completed border-free zone, would also be incorporated into the EU, lifting frontiers throughout the continent.
Britain, Ireland and Denmark would be given various opt-outs to meet their internal political concerns.
London and Dublin would retain their borders and the right to set their own visa, immigration and asylum policy.
Britain has argued that its island status makes its internal security policy different from the rest of the bloc. Ireland is linked to Britain through a passport union.
Denmark's opt-out reflects constitutional problems with passing sovereignty to EU institutions. As a Schengen member it is expected to remain part of the border-free zone.
On foreign and defence policy, two areas that EU integrationists had hoped would be beefed up, the leaders made minor changes to current policy.

Rather than adopt France's proposals for a high-profile foreign policy spokesman, the leaders agreed that the current secretary-general of the Council of Ministers would represent the EU in foreign policy.
Britain, Denmark and the bloc's neutrals -- Ireland, Austria, Finland and Sweden -- made sure that plans to integrate the Western European Union (WEU) defence group into the Union were blocked.

They were set to agree that the WEU would remain independent, sub-contracted to carry out humanitarian, peacekeeping and crisis management missions for the bloc "including peacemaking". All that remained in the EU treaty was language that the WEU "might in time" be integrated into the EU.
Leaders still faced some of the toughest issues, such as demands for flexibility -- the idea of letting some integrate faster that others.

A number of countries, worried that they will be left behind by eager integrationists, want individual member states to have a veto over such plans, but Germany, France and others are adamantly opposed to this.
The balance of power in institutions was also on the table -- a fight pitching the bloc's small countries against the largest.
